## VI Computational analysis

Now, let us move on to the numerical part and discuss in detail the complexity of using Bootstrap to deal with the quantum Hall problem. The complexity is essentially divided into two parts: the optimization problem itself (quantum Hall in our case) and the solver (algorithms used to solve the optimization problem). Thus, there are two parallel routes to improve efficiency: a better representation of the problem and a more robust and advanced solver. We will mainly focus on the first route, but will have a few comments regarding the second. In this section, we provide a detailed complexity analysis with actual running hours. We also introduce a physics-inspired simplification that allowed us to go to very large system sizes that are comparable to state-of-the-art sizes accessible to other methods such as DMRG.

### VI.1 Run time complexity

It should be noted that although a polynomial-time algorithm means a problem can be efficiently solved in principle, scaling as a polynomial with a high power or large prefactor can still make a problem intractable in practice (though in this case, we may hope that some tweaks on optimizations can go a long way into making it tractable). Thus, techniques like symmetry reductions that can reduce the power or prefactor of the computational scaling become extremely important. In the following complexity analysis, we will primarily consider the T2 constraints. Other constraints can be analyzed similarly.

With CMTS encoded and using the $S_{\bm{q}}$ representation, the SDP corresponding to T2 has the form of linear matrix inequality (LMI) with $N_{\Phi}^{2}$ variables (number of elements in $S_{\bm{q}}$ ) and a matrix dimension of $(N_{\Phi}-1)N_{\Phi}/2\times(N_{\Phi}-1)N_{\Phi}/2$ . From the standard convex optimization theory [102, 103], the time complexity using the primal-dual interior-point method is given by [62]

$$ O\left((m^{3}+m^{2}n^{2}+mn^{3})\sqrt{n}\log(1/\epsilon)\right), $$

where $m=N_{\Phi}^{2}$ , $n=(N_{\Phi}-1)N_{\Phi}/2$ and $\epsilon$ is tolerance for the duality gap. So, without any further optimization, bootstrapping the QH with the T2 constraint is roughly $O(N_{\Phi}^{9})$ hard [104]. This allows us to do $N_{\Phi}\sim$ 10s which can take us beyond ED, but makes $N_{\Phi}\sim$ 100 difficult to realize. The first and simplest optimization we did is to use the discrete symmetries to reduce the number of variables, i.e, the number independent elements in $S_{\bm{q}}$ . For example, since the ${\bm{q}}$ lattice is alway square, we can use the $C_{4}$ symmetry to reduce the number of variables by a factor 4. Further considering the mirror symmetry with mirror axes $q_{x,y}=0$ and $q_{x}=\pm q_{y}$ , we can reduce the number by a factor 8. Here we emphasize that this mirror isn’t a symmetry of the fractional quantum Hall state (magnetic field chooses a chirality) but a symmetry of the structure factor $S_{\bm{q}}=S_{|{\bm{q}}|}$ since the mirror actions preserve the norm $|{\bm{q}}|$ [105]. The results are summarized in Table 1. One should notice that the particle number $N$ doesn’t enter the complexity at all [106], so we did not include the information about the particle number in the table as it doesn’t change the run time too much.

### VI.2 $q$ -lattice sampling using approximated full rotational symmetry

The discrete symmetries discussed above only give us a constant reduction which does not change the scaling, meaning that the complexity is still $O(N_{\Phi}^{9})$ only now with a much smaller prefactor. On the other hand, to enable large-system calculation, we can employ other continuous symmetry of the quantum Hall problem as discussed below. Apart from CMTS, quantum Hall systems also have continuous rotation symmetry. This symmetry is broken on the torus but we expect it to be recovered in the limit of a sufficiently large torus. To account for this, we introduce the sampling method explained below.

Let us consider the structure factor $S_{\bm{q}}$ on a ${\bm{q}}$ lattice spanned by $\{-q_{x}^{max},-q_{x}^{max}+\Delta q_{x},\cdots,q_{x}^{max}\}$ and $\{-q_{y}^{max},-q_{y}^{max}+\Delta q_{y},\cdots,q_{y}^{max}\}$ . We want to sample $\kappa$ points from a line segment: $\{q_{1}=0,q_{2},q_{3},\cdots,q_{\kappa-1},q_{\kappa}=\sqrt{(q_{x}^{max})^{2}+(q_{y}^{max})^{2}}\}$ with $q_{i}$ ordered. We introduce a set of new optimization variables $\bm{S}=(S_{1},S_{2},\cdots,S_{\kappa})$ such that the original $S_{\bm{q}}$ can all be linearly interpolated from the new variables:

$$ S_{{\bm{q}}}=\frac{|{\bm{q}}|-q_{l}}{q_{r}-q_{l}}S_{l}+\frac{q_{r}-|{\bm{q}}|}{q_{r}-q_{l}}S_{r}, $$

where $r,l\in\{1,2,\cdots,\kappa\}$ and $q_{l}\leq|{\bm{q}}|\leq q_{r}$ with $q_{l,r}$ the two nearest neighbors of $|{\bm{q}}|$ . In doing so, the number of variables is reduced from $N_{\Phi}^{2}$ to $\kappa$ which is practically less than $N_{\Phi}$ . Thus, the complexity is also reduced to $O(N_{\Phi}^{8})$ .

One might be worried about the inaccuracy induced by this simplification, since it reliess on the full rotational symmetry and $S_{|{\bm{q}}|}$ being smooth. In fact, those two requirements are both approximately satisfied in quantum Hall on torus when the system size is sufficiently large. We tested this method with a uniform sampling of $N_{\Phi}$ points for a few system sizes. The result looks almost identical to the one using $C_{4}$ only with a difference of less than $10^{-4}$ in energy per particle. This allows us to perform very large system calculations as shown in Table 1. For example, the system size of $N_{\Phi}=11\times 11$ is translated to a circumference of $L_{y}=11\times\sqrt{2\pi}\approx 27$ in DMRG, which is comparable to state-of-the-art sizes achievable.

One final remark is that $S_{{\bm{q}}}$ has a fast-damping tail ( $S_{{\bm{q}}\to\infty}=S_{\infty}$ ). Furthermore, for any physical quantity, the large- ${\bm{q}}$ behavior is suppressed by the Gaussian factor $e^{-q^{2}/2}$ . Thus, when sampling the $S_{\kappa}$ , we can use less points for large $|q|$ without introducing any error in any physical observable such as energy or pair correlation function. This means, for very large systems, most of the ${\bm{q}}$ points are irrelevant with only few small ${\bm{q}}$ ’s needed. We call this the importance sampling. With this, $m$ can be further reduced from $N_{\Phi}^{2}$ to just $O(1)$ (a constant) leading to an $O(N_{\Phi}^{7})$ time complexity.

### VI.3 SDP solvers

The above analysis is based on the primal-dual interior-point method [62] which is a second-order algorithm and used in most of the modern SDP solvers like MOSEK [64] or COPT [101] since it is the most robust algorithm applicable to all kinds of SDPs. However, it doesn’t necessarily mean that it is the best algorithm for quantum many-body bootstrap using the RDM theory. In fact, it has been demonstrated that a first-order algorithm called boundary-point method can improve the efficiency by at least one order-of-magnitude for RDM calculations in quantum chemistry comparing to the interior-point method [107]. We believe that developing a special solver for quantum many-body bootstrap will enable a similar speedup, that will enable us to access even larger system sizes and impose more constraints.

## VII Discussion and Outlook

### VII.1 Nature of correlation functions

We begin by discussing a few subtleties and caveats regarding this method, particularly when used to compute ground state correlation functions (static structure factor in our case). While conventional variational method search a subset of valid physical states and thus always outputs a physically realizable correlation function, even if it is not the correct one for the ground state, this method searches a superset of valid physical correlation functions and thus its output is not always associated with any physical state. However, by enforcing enough constraints we can make sure these correlation functions are not easily distinguishable from physical ones, since if there was a computationally simple way to check that the obtained correlation is unphysical, we can add it to our set of constraints (at least if it has PSD form). This suggests that the more constraints we include, the harder it will be to distinguish the results we get from physical correlation functions. Our results on the quantum Hall problem suggest that our structure factors approximate the physical ones to a good degree. We leave a more rigorous discussion of how the output of this method approaches physical correlation functions to future works.

One feature we may expect in the output of this method is the following. If there are two closely competing states A and B, we may get some ‘compromise’ correlation functions that combine energetically favorable features of both states, even if there is no physical state with both features. As the constraints get tighter, the method will be forced to choose the correlation function corresponding to one of the states. This may help explain some of the features of our results; the extra fluctuations at large ${\bm{r}}$ in $g({\bm{r}})$ at $\nu=1/3$ (Fig. 3) may be associated with correlations of a nearby CFL or a Wigner crystal. This is perhaps because the $\nu=\frac{1}{4}$ CFL optimizes $V_{3}$ in the degenerate space annihilated by $V_{1}$ , and the bootstrap constraints are not yet tight enough to select out Laughlin as the unique zero mode of $V_{1}$ at $\nu=\frac{1}{3}$ . Another option is a competitor Wigner crystal state, which in reality cannot be a zero mode of $V_{1}$ like the state in the bootstrap [108]. This picture suggests that constraints which rule out such compromise correlation functions between closely competing states can help significantly improve the results.

### VII.3 Further extensions: 3RDM

One limitation of the 2-RDM approach discussed here is that constraints beyond (2,2), T1 and Generalized T2 requite tensor factorization of the variables and thus do not have the form of PSD constraints. While there are possible approaches to deal with this limitation, which will be the topic for follow-up work, a straightforward way to go beyond our results is to consider higher RDMs. In this approach, instead of combining higher-body operators to produce a 2-body operator, we directly impose positivity constraints on the higher-body operators. Clearly, this approach is more memory intensive; 3RDM positivity constraints (namely, the (3,3) constraints) involve $O(N_{\Phi}^{4})$ after accounting for CMTS. In fact, due to fermionic antisymmetry, the number of optimization variables is in practice $\sim 0.03N_{\Phi}^{4}$ , making it achievable for reasonable system sizes.

While an elaborate discussion about the higher RDM constraints will be given elsewhere, we provide the energy comparison in Fig. 9, which shows modest improvement compared to the T1/T2 constraints used in this work. The improvement in the relative error is largest for small fillings. Interestingly, our (2,3) results approach the full (3,3) for fillings close to $\nu=1/2$ . This can be understood by noting that particle-hole symmetry makes $\langle c^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}ccc\rangle$ equivalent to $\langle cccc^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}\rangle$ at exactly half filling, thus indicating that the (2,3)-T1 and T2 combined are equivalent to the full (3,3) constraints. Note however that the 3RDM positivity constraints are still not sufficiently strong to fix the shift of the charge gap (as shown in the lower panel in Fig. 9), suggesting the need of different constraints as we argued earlier.

It is worth mentioning that it is possible to formulate a dual version of the RDM optimization [39, 40], where the constraints become the optimization variables and RDM plays the role of a Lagrange multiplier. The main simplification in this formulation relies on the observation that for any solution of the optimization problem, only a small number of constraints is saturated or “active” (these will correspond to zero eigenvalues of the PSD constraint matrices). Furthermore, since the solution always lies on the boundary of the feasible region, there is a simple geometric meaning for those active constraints e.g. if there is only one active constraint, it has to describe the plane tangent to the feasible region which is perpendicular to the direction of the Hamiltonian. We leave a detailed discussion of such formulation to follow-up works.

### VII.4 Higher constraints, convergence and approximations

One important consideration for future works is to develop a more systematic understanding of the convergence of both the structure factor (or more generally the 2RDM) and the energy as we add more constraints and of the kinds of constraints that are best for capturing certain states. We speculate that the $(2,2)$ and $(2,3)$ constraints capture 2-particle and 3-particle correlations to a large extent, leading to accurate ground state properties for states whose main correlations are 2- and 3-body correlations. The prominence of few body correlations is expected since the projected Coulomb Hamiltonian itself is a two-body Hamiltonian. However, there may be more filling-dependent global configurational constraints arising from the structure of the Hilbert space that are not encoded in these constraints, or at least are only encoded on average. One route to understand $(2,p)$ constraints is by viewing them as positivity constraints on 2-body dual Hamiltonians acting on some $p$ -particle wavefunctions belonging to a constrained space. While the computational cost for such $(2,p)$ constraints increases with $p$ , good approximations of such constraints can be implemented far more efficiently if we can find a good variational ansatz for the space of low energy states of the corresponding Hamiltonian.

### VII.5 Constraints beyond the $(2,p)$ hierarchy

While we have focused on deriving energetic lower bounds, several generalizations of this approach employed in the context of quantum mechanical bootstrap [25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 33] can also give information about the spectrum and provide bounds on correlation functions. One is to replace the energy minimization by the constraints $\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle=E$ and $\langle\mathcal{H}\mathcal{O}\rangle=\langle\mathcal{O}\mathcal{H}\rangle=E\langle\mathcal{O}\rangle$ for any operator $\mathcal{O}$ , which has the effect of restricting to eigenstates of the Hamiltonian. This could potentially yield discrete windows of possible values of the energy [33]. For the LLL, the simplest choice for $\mathcal{O}$ involves a product of projected densities $\rho_{\bm{p}}\rho_{-{\bm{p}}}$ . Such a condition provides a constraint on the 4-RDM rather than the 2RDM. The weaker condition $\langle[\mathcal{H},\mathcal{O}]\rangle=0$ leads to a constraint on the 3-RDM. For more general band systems lacking CMTS, choosing $\mathcal{O}=c^{\dagger}_{\alpha}c_{\beta}$ would lead to constraints on the 3-RDM (using $\langle\mathcal{H}\mathcal{O}\rangle=\langle\mathcal{O}\mathcal{H}\rangle=E\langle\mathcal{O}\rangle$ ) and 2RDM ( $\langle[\mathcal{H},\mathcal{O}]\rangle=0$ ). Such constraints are normally referred to the equation of motion (EoM) constraints since it selects the possible eigenstates of the Hamiltonian [25].

Another possible approach is to notice that the ground state energy cannot be lowered by applying any operator, which implies $\langle\mathcal{O}^{\dagger}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{O}\rangle\geq E\langle\mathcal{O}^{\dagger}\mathcal{O}\rangle$ for expectation values evaluated in the ground state. Combined with $\langle\mathcal{H}\mathcal{O}\rangle=E\langle\mathcal{O}\rangle$ which holds for any eigenstate, we get the relation $\langle\mathcal{O}^{\dagger}[\mathcal{H},\mathcal{O}]\rangle\geq 0$ . If the operator $\mathcal{O}$ can be expanded by a set of basis operators $\{\mathcal{O}_{i}\}$ such that $\mathcal{O}=\sum_{i}A_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}$ , then the positivity becomes a PSD constraint:

$$ \mathcal{C}\succeq 0,\quad\mathcal{C}_{ij}\equiv\langle\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\dagger}[\mathcal{H},\mathcal{O}_{j}]\rangle, $$

since we have $\langle\mathcal{O}^{\dagger}[\mathcal{H},\mathcal{O}]\rangle=\sum_{ij}A^{*}_{i}\mathcal{C}_{ij}A_{j}\geq 0,\text{ }\forall A$ . This PSD constraint is called the perturbative positivity that selects (only works for) the ground state (note that the DQG/T1/T2 conditions work for any possible states include the excited states). When considering operators $\mathcal{O}$ for perturbative positivity constraints, it is important to keep track of the number of particles involved since we are studying systems with fixed particle number. For operators which change particle number, such constraints will relate ground state properties at different fillings. We can avoid this by focusing on operators that do not change the particle number. Thus, the choices for $\{\mathcal{O}\}$ are limited to the zero particle basis: order-2 basis $\{c^{\dagger}_{\alpha}c_{\beta}\}$ (or $\{\rho_{\bm{q}}\}$ if the form factor matrix is invertible); order-4 basis $\{c^{\dagger}_{\alpha}c^{\dagger}_{\beta}c_{\delta}c_{\gamma},c^{\dagger}_{\alpha}c_{\beta}\}$ ; and so on. A weaker version of this perturbative positivity is to take the double commutator: $\langle[\mathcal{O}^{\dagger},[\mathcal{H},\mathcal{O}]]\rangle\geq 0$ which will lower the order of RDMs involved by one. For example, if we choose $\{\mathcal{O}\}$ to be $\{\rho_{\bm{q}}\}$ , combining CMTS and GMP algebra, we have the following constraint on the structure factor:

$$ \int\frac{d^{2}{\bm{p}}}{2\pi}V_{\bm{p}}e^{-\frac{p^{2}}{2}}\sin^{2}\frac{{\bm{p}}\wedge{\bm{q}}}{2}(S_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{p}}}-S_{\bm{p}})\geq 0\quad\forall{\bm{q}}. $$

We tested these constraints and found that they do not lead to tighter lower bounds on energy compared to the positivity constraints we use, but they lead to upper bounds on the ground state energy since the perturbative positivity selects the ground state excluding excited states. We found these bounds to be a lot looser than known variational bounds for the simplest operators we tried, but they will likely get tighter as we impose more constraints. Nevertheless, this shows the great potential to get two-side bounds purely from Bootstrap (see also Ref. [109] for a related discussion). We leave a detailed discussion of these more general bounds to future works. We also note recent attempts aiming to generalize this approach to finite temperatures [110, 111, 109].

### VII.6 Higher Landau levels and Chern bands

A few obvious extensions of this work include (i) higher Landau levels, (ii) bosonic quantum Hall states, and (iii) correlated states in topological flat bands. Direction (i) is the most obvious generalization and can be implemented through the simple replacement $V_{\bm{q}}\mapsto V_{\bm{q}}[L_{n}({\bm{q}}^{2}/2)]^{2}$ . In higher LLs, both non-Abelian states and symmetry broken states such as stripes and Wigner crystals are expected [112, 113, 114]. Detecting these phases through the structure factor is possible but requires more careful analysis of its dependence as a function of geometry and system size [113, 114]. For direction (ii), we can still employ the Haldane duality and the $(2,2)$ constraints but there is no simple analog of the higher $(2,p)$ constraints. One possibility to address this is to include higher RDMs as variables in the bootstrap approach. For direction (iii), the main difference is the absence of CMTS which means that $\langle\rho_{\bm{q}}\rho_{-{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}\rangle$ is in general non-vanishing for any reciprocal lattice vector ${\bm{G}}$ . As discussed in the main text, we can still derive some version of the Haldane duality under some assumptions that remain to hold for bands which are sufficiently close to the LLL. For bands where the generalized Haldane duality does not hold, we can still perform the bootstrap by using the 2RDM instead of the structure factor. Note that single particle dispersion may also be included, as its expectation value also only depends on the 2RDM.

## Appendix A Upper bounds from variational Monte Carlo

In this section, we provide the details about the upper bound calculations using variational Monte Carlo (VMC) with model wavefunctions. The method used is called the lattice Monte Carlo for quantum Hall on torus developed by one of us [68]. We will not discuss any of the technical details of that method for which the reader is encouraged to read Ref. [68]. Here, we outline the model wavefunctions used for the VMC.

First, for the $\nu=1/m$ Laughlin state, the model wavefunction on torus is given by [115]

$$ \Psi_{\text{Laughlin}}(\{\alpha\})=\prod_{i<j}^{N}\left[f(z_{i}-z_{j})\right]^{m}\prod_{k=1}^{m}f(Z-\alpha_{k}), $$

where $z=x+iy$ is the complexified electron coordinate, $Z=\sum_{i}^{N}z_{i}$ is the center-of-mass, $\alpha_{k}$ ’s $(k=1,\cdots,m)$ are the center-of-mass zeros that encode the periodic boundary condition by requiring $\sum_{k=1}^{m}\alpha_{k}=0\mod\text{BZ}$ , and $f(z)=\sigma(z|a_{1},a_{2})\exp{-\frac{1}{N_\Phi}zz^*}$ with $\sigma(z|a_{1},a_{2})$ the “modified Weierstrass sigma function” [116] ( $a_{1},a_{2}$ are two complex vectors defining the unit cell, i.e, the lattice constants).

Then, for the CFL state ( $\nu=1/m$ with $m$ even), there are a few model states proposed [74, 93, 117]. We will use the one in Ref. [68] which is more favorable for Monte Carlo calculations. It is given by [118, 119]

$$ \Psi_{\text{CFL}}(\{\alpha\},\{d\})=\det\tilde{M}_{ij}\prod_{i<j}\left[f(z_{i}-z_{j})\right]^{m-2}\prod_{k=1}^{m}f(Z-\alpha_{k}), $$

where $\tilde{M}_{ij}$ is a $N\times N$ matrix:

$$ \tilde{M}_{ij}=e^{\frac{1}{2m}(z_{i}d_{j}^{*}-z_{i}^{*}d_{j})}\prod_{k\neq j}^{N}f(z_{i}-z_{k}-d_{j}+\bar{d}), $$

with $\det\tilde{M}_{ij}$ its determinant. In addition to a dependence on the $m$ center of mass zeros $\{\alpha\}$ , this wave function depends on $N$ additional parameters $\{d\}$ , the dipole moments.

## Supplemental Material

This supplementary material contains detailed discussions on momentum space formulation of the QH problem and the Bootstrapping constraints.

### A.1 Bloch states in the LLL and form factors

We can define the magnetic translation operator $T_{\bm{u}}=e^{-i{\bm{u}}\wedge{\bm{R}}}$ . Using the commutation relations of the guiding center $[R_{\alpha},R_{\beta}]=-i\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}$ , it is straightforward to show that this operator satisfies the magnetic algebra

$$ T_{\bm{u}}T_{\bm{v}}=e^{\frac{i}{2}{\bm{u}}\wedge{\bm{v}}}T_{{\bm{u}}+{\bm{v}}}=e^{i{\bm{u}}\wedge{\bm{v}}}T_{{\bm{v}}}T_{{\bm{u}}} $$

Here, we used the notation $\wedge{\bm{v}}=(v_{y},-v_{x})$ and ${\bm{u}}\wedge{\bm{v}}={\bm{u}}\cdot(\wedge{\bm{v}})=u_{x}v_{y}-u_{y}v_{x}$ . Note that the magnetic translation operator is related to the form factor matrix via $\Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{\alpha\beta}=\langle\alpha|T_{\wedge{\bm{q}}}|\beta\rangle$ .

To express the form factor in momentum space, let us define a unit cell containing $2\pi$ flux spanned by the vectors ${\bm{a}}_{1}$ and ${\bm{a}}_{2}$ such that $|{\bm{a}}_{1}\wedge{\bm{a}}_{2}|=2\pi$ . Then for any lattice vectors ${\bm{a}}=n{\bm{a}}_{1}+m{\bm{a}}_{2}$ and ${\bm{a}}^{\prime}=n^{\prime}{\bm{a}}_{1}+m^{\prime}{\bm{a}}_{2}$ , the magnetic translation operators commute $[T_{\bm{a}},T_{{\bm{a}}^{\prime}}]=0$ . As a result, they can be simultaneously diagonalized with the eigenstates corresponding to the Bloch states defined via

$$ T_{\bm{a}}\psi_{\bm{k}}=\eta_{\bm{a}}e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{a}}}\psi_{\bm{k}} $$

where the factor $\eta_{\bm{a}}$ , introduced for latter convenience, is $+1$ if ${\bm{a}}/2$ is a lattice vector and $-1$ otherwise. The explicit action of $T_{\bm{u}}$ in real space is can be chosen to be $T_{\bm{u}}f({\bm{r}})=e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{u}}\wedge{\bm{r}}}f({\bm{r}}+{\bm{u}})$ . Thus, the Bloch states take the form

$$ \psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}})=Ce^{\frac{i}{2}\bar{k}r}\sigma(r+ik|a_{1},a_{2})e^{-\frac{1}{4}r\bar{r}}e^{-\frac{1}{4}k\bar{k}} $$

where $C$ is an unimportant normalization constant. Here, we use the notation that the complexified version of a variable is denoted by unbolded letter, e.g. $r=r_{x}+ir_{y}$ , $k=k_{x}+ik_{y}$ and $\sigma(z|a_{1},a_{2})$ is the modified Weierstrass sigma function with lattice parameters $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ which satisfies

$$ \sigma(z+a|a_{1},a_{2})=\eta_{\bm{a}}e^{\frac{\bar{a}}{2}(z+\frac{a}{2})}\sigma(z|a_{1},a_{2}),\qquad\sigma(-z)=-\sigma(z) $$

In what follows, we will drop the lattice parameters and use the simplified notation $\sigma(z):=\sigma(z|a_{1},a_{2})$ .

It is easy to see using (S4) that Bloch states (S3) satisfy

$$ \psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}}+{\bm{a}})=\eta_{\bm{a}}e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{a}}}e^{\frac{i}{2}{\bm{a}}\wedge{\bm{r}}}\phi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}}),\qquad\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}}({\bm{r}})=\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{\frac{i}{2}{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}}) $$

In the Bloch basis, the form factor is given by $\Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}=\langle\psi_{{\bm{k}}}|e^{-i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}|\psi_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle$ . Now notice that $T_{\bm{u}}e^{i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}=T_{\bm{u}}T_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}=e^{i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{u}}}e^{i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}T_{\bm{u}}$ which means that $T_{\bm{a}}[e^{i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\psi_{{\bm{k}}}]=\eta_{\bm{a}}e^{i({\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}})\cdot{\bm{a}}}e^{i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\psi_{{\bm{k}}}$ . Thus, since we are considering a single non-degenerate band $e^{i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\psi_{{\bm{k}}}$ should be proportional to $\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}$ . The proportionality constant (which generally depends on both ${\bm{k}}$ and ${\bm{q}}$ ) can be determined from the explicit form of the Bloch wavefunctions (S3) as

$$ \displaystyle e^{i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}}) \displaystyle=T_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}})=Ce^{\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{r}}}e^{\frac{i}{2}\bar{k}(r+iq)}\sigma(r+i(k+q)|a_{1},a_{2})e^{-\frac{1}{4}(r+iq)(\bar{r}-i\bar{q})}e^{-\frac{1}{4}k\bar{k}} \displaystyle=Ce^{\frac{i}{2}r(\bar{k}+\bar{q})}\sigma(r+i(k+q)|a_{1},a_{2})e^{-\frac{1}{4}r\bar{r}}e^{-\frac{1}{4}k\bar{k}}e^{-\frac{1}{4}q\bar{q}-\frac{1}{2}q\bar{k}}=\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}({\bm{r}})e^{\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}, $$

which leads to the form factor $\Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}=\langle e^{i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}|\psi_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\langle\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}|\psi_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle$ . Note that $|\psi_{\bm{k}}\rangle$ and $|\psi_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle$ are not orthogonal unless we restrict ${\bm{k}}$ and ${\bm{k}}^{\prime}$ to the first BZ (if ${\bm{k}}^{\prime}={\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}$ , clearly $\langle\psi_{{\bm{k}}}|\psi_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{i{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\neq 0$ ). Let us denote by $[{\bm{k}}]$ the part of ${\bm{k}}$ within the first BZ and by $\{{\bm{k}}\}:={\bm{k}}-[{\bm{k}}]$ its reciprocal lattice part. Using Eq. S5, we can write $|\psi_{\bm{k}}\rangle=\alpha^{*}_{\bm{k}}|\psi_{[{\bm{k}}]}\rangle$ where $\alpha_{\bm{k}}=\eta_{\{{\bm{k}}\}}e^{\frac{i}{2}[{\bm{k}}]\wedge\{{\bm{k}}\}}$ which leads to the expression of the form factor

$$ \Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}=e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\langle\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}|\psi_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\alpha^{*}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\alpha_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\delta_{[{\bm{k}}^{\prime}],[{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}]} $$

Notice that the form factor is not gauge invariant. Instead, it changes by $\Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\mapsto\Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}e^{i[\phi({\bm{k}}^{\prime})-\phi({\bm{k}})]}$ under the gauge transformation $\psi_{\bm{k}}\mapsto e^{i\phi({\bm{k}})}\psi_{\bm{k}}$ . We will find it convenient to choose a periodic gauge corresponding to the wavefunctions

$$ |\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}}\rangle\equiv\alpha_{{\bm{k}}}|\psi_{\bm{k}}\rangle=|\psi_{[{\bm{k}}]}\rangle $$

which is manifestly periodic in ${\bm{k}}$ since it depends only on $[{\bm{k}}]$ . The form factors in the periodic gauge become

$$ \Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}=e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\alpha_{\bm{k}}^{*}\alpha_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\langle\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}|\psi_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\alpha^{*}_{{\bm{k}}}\alpha_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\delta_{[{\bm{k}}^{\prime}],[{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}]}=\lambda_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})\delta_{[{\bm{k}}^{\prime}],[{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}]},\qquad\lambda_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})=e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\alpha^{*}_{{\bm{k}}}\alpha_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}} $$

This expression is manifestly invariant under ${\bm{k}}^{\prime}\mapsto{\bm{k}}^{\prime}+{\bm{G}}$ for any reciprocal lattice vector ${\bm{G}}$ . To show it is also periodic in ${\bm{k}}$ , note that for any reciprocal lattice vectors $e^{\pm\frac{i}{2}{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{G}}^{\prime}}=\eta_{\bm{G}}\eta_{{\bm{G}}^{\prime}}\eta_{{\bm{G}}+{\bm{G}}^{\prime}}$ which implies

$$ \alpha_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}}=\eta_{\{{\bm{k}}\}}\eta_{\{{\bm{k}}\}+{\bm{G}}}e^{\frac{i}{2}[{\bm{k}}]\wedge{\bm{G}}}\alpha_{{\bm{k}}}=\eta_{{\bm{G}}}e^{\frac{i}{2}{\bm{k}}\wedge{\bm{G}}}\alpha_{{\bm{k}}}, $$

leading to the identities

$$ \lambda_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}})=\lambda_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})\qquad\lambda_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}({\bm{k}})=\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{G}}}e^{-i{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\lambda_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}). $$

### A.2 Continuous magnetic translation symmetry (CMTS)

The action of magnetic translation symmetry in the periodic gauge is

$$ T_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}}({\bm{r}})=\alpha_{\bm{k}}T_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}})=\alpha_{\bm{k}}\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}({\bm{r}})e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{k}}\wedge{\bm{q}}}\\
=\alpha_{\bm{k}}\alpha^{*}_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{k}}\wedge{\bm{q}}}\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}({\bm{r}}) $$

by noting that $\alpha_{[{\bm{k}}]}=1$ .

To see how the second-quantized operator transforms under the magnetic translation, we first look at the transformation of a single fermion operator in position space:

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\bm{u}}^{-1}c_{\bm{r}}\mathcal{T}_{\bm{u}}=e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{u}}\wedge{\bm{r}}}c_{{\bm{r}}+{\bm{u}}}=T_{\bm{u}}c_{\bm{r}}. $$

We can then expand $c_{\bm{r}}$ using the momentum basis:

$$ c_{\bm{r}}=\sum_{{\bm{k}}\in\text{BZ}}\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}}({\bm{r}})c_{\bm{k}}\quad\text{ with }\quad c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}}=c_{\bm{k}}. $$

Thus, the magnetic translation becomes

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{{\bm{k}}\in\text{BZ}}\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}}({\bm{r}})\mathcal{T}_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}^{-1}c_{\bm{k}}\mathcal{T}_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{k}}\in\text{BZ}}\left[T_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}}({\bm{r}})\right]c_{\bm{k}}=\sum_{{\bm{k}}\in\text{BZ}}\alpha_{\bm{k}}\alpha^{*}_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{k}}\wedge{\bm{q}}}\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}({\bm{r}})c_{\bm{k}} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{k}}\in\text{BZ}}\lambda^{*}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}({\bm{r}})c_{\bm{k}}=\sum_{{\bm{k}}\in\text{BZ}}\lambda^{*}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}})\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}}({\bm{r}})c_{{\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}}}=\sum_{{\bm{k}}\in\text{BZ}}\lambda_{-{\bm{q}}}({\bm{k}})\tilde{\psi}_{{\bm{k}}}({\bm{r}})c_{{\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}}} $$

which implies

$$ \mathcal{T}_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}^{-1}c_{\bm{k}}\mathcal{T}_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}=\lambda_{-{\bm{q}}}({\bm{k}})c_{{\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}}}\equiv\beta_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{q}}}c_{{\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}}}. $$

Similarly, we have

$$ \mathcal{T}_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}^{-1}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\mathcal{T}_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}=\beta^{*}_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{q}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}}}. $$

Now, let us discuss the continuous magnetic translation symmetry (CMTS) for the density matrices. First we define the density operator in the following way:

$$ \hat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}=d^{\dagger}_{\sigma_{1},{\bm{k}}_{1}}\cdots d^{\dagger}_{\sigma_{n},{\bm{k}}_{n}}d_{\sigma_{n},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{n}}\cdots d_{\sigma_{1},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}}, $$

where $\sigma_{i}=\pm$ for $i=1,\cdots,n$ and $d_{+,{\bm{k}}}=c_{\bm{k}}$ and $d_{-,{\bm{k}}}=c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}}$ . Thus, the CMTS in terms of $d$ ’s becomes

$$ \mathcal{T}_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}^{-1}d_{\sigma,{\bm{k}}}\mathcal{T}_{-\wedge{\bm{q}}}=\beta^{\sigma}_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{q}}}d_{\sigma,{\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}}}\quad\text{ with }\quad\beta^{+}=\beta\text{ and }\beta^{-}=\beta^{*}. $$

We can call this density operator the order $(n-m,m)$ density operator and denote it as $\hat{\mathcal{D}}^{(n,m)}$ , where $m=\sum_{l=1}^{n}(|\sigma_{l}|+\sigma_{l})/2$ . It is not hard to see that the density operator is not invariant under the continuous magnetic translation. We have to look at the physical state that is invariant under such transformation. Given a state $|\Psi\rangle$ such that

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\bm{u}}|\Psi\rangle=e^{i\theta_{\bm{u}}}|\Psi\rangle, $$

we should have

$$ \langle\Psi|\mathcal{T}_{\bm{u}}^{-1}\hat{\mathcal{D}}^{(n,m)}\mathcal{T}_{\bm{u}}|\Psi\rangle=\langle\Psi|e^{-i\theta_{\bm{u}}}\hat{\mathcal{D}}^{(n,m)}e^{i\theta_{\bm{u}}}|\Psi\rangle=\langle\Psi|\hat{\mathcal{D}}^{(n,m)}|\Psi\rangle, $$

which gives the CMTS in the primal form.

Now, if the ground state $|\Omega\rangle$ of the system doesn’t spontaneously break the CMTS [122], we can define the density matrix in momentum space corresponding to $\hat{\mathcal{D}}^{(n,m)}$ as

$$ \mathcal{M}^{(n,m)}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},\cdots,{\bm{k}}_{n};{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},\cdots,{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{n}}\equiv\langle\Omega|d^{\dagger}_{\sigma_{1},{\bm{k}}_{1}}\cdots d^{\dagger}_{\sigma_{n},{\bm{k}}_{n}}d_{\sigma_{n},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{n}}\cdots d_{\sigma_{1},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}}|\Omega\rangle. $$

The CMTS then implies that

$$ \mathcal{M}^{(n,m)}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},\cdots,{\bm{k}}_{n};{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},\cdots,{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{n}}=\left[\prod_{l=1}^{n}\left(\beta^{\sigma_{l}}_{{\bm{k}}_{l},{\bm{q}}}\right)^{*}\beta^{\sigma_{l}}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{l},{\bm{q}}}\right]\mathcal{M}^{(n,m)}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{q}},\cdots,{\bm{k}}_{n}-{\bm{q}};{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}-{\bm{q}},\cdots,{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{n}-{\bm{q}}} $$

If we further consider the crystal momentum conservation, we can define the total momentum ${\bm{Q}}$ as

$$ {\bm{Q}}=\left[\sum_{l=1}^{n}\sigma_{l}{\bm{k}}_{l}\right]=\left[\sum_{l=1}^{n}\sigma_{l}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{l}\right], $$

thus we can eliminate two momentum variables from the two equalities above:

$$ {\bm{k}}_{n}=\sigma_{n}\left[{\bm{Q}}-\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}\sigma_{l}{\bm{k}}_{l}\right]\quad\text{ and }\quad{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{n}=\sigma_{n}\left[{\bm{Q}}-\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}\sigma_{l}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{l}\right]. $$

Substitute into Eq. (S23), we have the transformation between different momentum sectors:

$$ \begin{split}&\mathcal{M}^{(n,m),{\bm{Q}}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},\cdots,{\bm{k}}_{n-1};{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},\cdots,{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{n-1}}\\
&=\left(\beta^{\sigma_{n}}_{\sigma_{n}[{\bm{Q}}-\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}\sigma_{l}{\bm{k}}_{l}],{\bm{q}}}\right)^{*}\beta^{\sigma_{n}}_{\sigma_{n}[{\bm{Q}}-\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}\sigma_{l}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{l}],{\bm{q}}}\left[\prod_{l=1}^{n-1}\left(\beta^{\sigma_{l}}_{{\bm{k}}_{l},{\bm{q}}}\right)^{*}\beta^{\sigma_{l}}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{l},{\bm{q}}}\right]\mathcal{M}^{(n,m),[{\bm{Q}}-(2m-n){\bm{q}}]}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{q}},\cdots,{\bm{k}}_{n-1}-{\bm{q}};{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}-{\bm{q}},\cdots,{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{n-1}-{\bm{q}}}.\end{split} $$

Although the mapping looks complicated, it simply states that the two matrices are related in the following way:

$$ \mathcal{M}^{(n,m),{\bm{Q}}}({\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime})=\mathcal{U}^{{\bm{Q}}\dagger}({\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime})\mathcal{M}^{(n,m),[{\bm{Q}}-(2m-n){\bm{q}}]}({\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}-{\bm{q}})\mathcal{U}^{\bm{Q}}({\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}), $$

where ${\bm{k}}=\{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2},\cdots,{\bm{k}}_{n-1}\}$ and $\mathcal{U}^{\bm{Q}}$ is a diagonal unitary matrix in the indices $({\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime})$ . Notice that both the constant index shifting and the unitary transformation cannot change the spectrum of a matrix. Thus, under the CMTS, $\mathcal{M}^{(n,m),{\bm{Q}}}$ and $\mathcal{M}^{(n,m),[{\bm{Q}}-(2m-n){\bm{q}}]}$ have exactly the same spectrum.

### A.3 Momentum space formulation of the $(2,p)$ constraints

In this section, we show in detail how to write the positivity constraints on a momentum basis.

#### A.3.1 Inverse form factor matrix for 0 ${}^{\text{th}}$ LL and (2,2) positivity constraints

Given that in the momentum space

$$ \rho_{\bm{q}}=\sum_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\lambda_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})=e^{-\frac{1}{4}{\bm{q}}^{2}}\sum_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})\equiv e^{-\frac{1}{4}{\bm{q}}^{2}}\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}}, $$

or equivalently,

$$ \tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}}=\sum_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\quad\text{with}\quad\Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\equiv\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}-{\bm{k}}^{\prime}],0}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}), $$

we shall have

$$ \tilde{\rho}_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}=\sum_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\tilde{\lambda}_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}({\bm{k}})=\sum_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{-i{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}+\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{G}}}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}), $$

where we used

$$ \begin{split}\tilde{\lambda}_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}({\bm{k}})&=e^{-\frac{i}{2}({\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}})\wedge{\bm{k}}}\alpha^{*}_{\bm{k}}\alpha_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}=e^{-\frac{i}{2}({\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}})\wedge{\bm{k}}}\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{\frac{i}{2}({\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}})\wedge{\bm{G}}}\alpha^{*}_{\bm{k}}\alpha_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\\
&=\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{-i{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}+\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{G}}}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}).\end{split} $$

This then leads to

$$ \tilde{\rho}_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{G}}}=\sum_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}e^{-i{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}). $$

Multiplying both sides by $e^{i{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}^{*}({\bm{k}}^{\prime})/N_{\bm{G}}$ ( $N_{\bm{G}}=N_{\Phi}$ in this case) and summing over ${\bm{G}}$ , we get

$$ \begin{split}\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{\bm{G}}e^{i{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\tilde{\rho}_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{G}}}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}^{*}({\bm{k}}^{\prime})=&\sum_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}^{*}({\bm{k}}^{\prime})\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{\bm{G}}e^{i{\bm{G}}\wedge({\bm{k}}^{\prime}-{\bm{k}})}\\
=&\sum_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})\lambda_{\bm{q}}^{*}({\bm{k}}^{\prime})\delta_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\\
=&c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}c_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}+{\bm{q}}},\end{split} $$

where we have used the fact that $\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{\bm{G}}e^{i{\bm{G}}\wedge({\bm{k}}^{\prime}-{\bm{k}})}=\delta_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}$ and $|\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})|=1$ by construction. Notice that $c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\equiv c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}+[{\bm{q}}]}$ on the right-hand side, we can restrict ${\bm{q}}$ to be within the first BZ and let ${\bm{q}}^{\prime}\equiv{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}$ to be the unrestricted momentum (thus, ${\bm{q}}=[{\bm{q}}]$ and ${\bm{G}}=\{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}\}$ ). By doing this, the above equation can be rewritten in the following form:

$$ \begin{split}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}}c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}=\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}^{\prime}-{\bm{q}}],0}e^{i\{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}\}\wedge{\bm{k}}}\tilde{\rho}_{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}\eta_{\{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}\}}e^{-\frac{i}{2}[{\bm{q}}^{\prime}]\wedge\{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}\}}\lambda_{[{\bm{q}}^{\prime}]}^{*}({\bm{k}}).\end{split} $$

Then, let ${\bm{k}}^{\prime}={\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}$ , we can further adopt a matrix form for such expression:

$$ c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}}c_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}=\sum_{\bm{q}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}} $$

with the matrix $\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}$ defined as

$$ \begin{split}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\equiv&\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}-({\bm{k}}^{\prime}-{\bm{k}})],0}e^{i\{{\bm{q}}\}\wedge{\bm{k}}}e^{-\frac{i}{2}[{\bm{q}}]\wedge\{{\bm{q}}\}}\eta_{\{{\bm{q}}\}}\tilde{\lambda}_{[{\bm{q}}]}^{*}({\bm{k}})\\
=&\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}-{\bm{k}}^{\prime}],0}\tilde{\lambda}_{{\bm{q}}}^{*}({\bm{k}}).\end{split} $$

One can check that

$$ \begin{split}\sum_{\bm{q}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda_{\bm{q}}^{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}=&\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}_{1})\tilde{\lambda}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}_{3})\\
=&\sum_{[{\bm{q}}]}\delta_{[[{\bm{q}}]+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\delta_{[[{\bm{q}}]+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{\bm{G}}\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{[{\bm{q}}]+{\bm{G}}}({\bm{k}}_{1})\tilde{\lambda}_{[{\bm{q}}]+{\bm{G}}}({\bm{k}}_{3})\\
=&\sum_{[{\bm{q}}]}\delta_{[[{\bm{q}}]+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\delta_{[[{\bm{q}}]+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{[{\bm{q}}]}({\bm{k}}_{1})\tilde{\lambda}_{[{\bm{q}}]}({\bm{k}}_{3})\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{\bm{G}}e^{i{\bm{G}}\wedge({\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{3})}\\
=&\sum_{[{\bm{q}}]}\delta_{[[{\bm{q}}]+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\delta_{[[{\bm{q}}]+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}=\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{4}}.\end{split} $$

and

$$ \begin{split}\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda_{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}^{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}=&\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}^{\prime}+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}_{1})\tilde{\lambda}_{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}({\bm{k}}_{1})\\
=&\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}-{\bm{q}}^{\prime}],0}\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}_{1})\tilde{\lambda}_{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}({\bm{k}}_{1})\\
=&\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}-{\bm{q}}^{\prime}],0}\sum_{\bm{G}}\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}_{1})\tilde{\lambda}_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{G}}}({\bm{k}}_{1})\delta_{{\bm{G}},\{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}-{\bm{q}}\}}\\
=&\delta_{[{\bm{q}}-{\bm{q}}^{\prime}],0}\sum_{\bm{G}}\delta_{{\bm{G}},\{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}-{\bm{q}}\}}\frac{1}{N_{\bm{G}}}\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}\eta_{\bm{G}}e^{i{\bm{G}}\wedge{\bm{k}}_{1}-\frac{i}{2}{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{G}}}\\
=&\delta_{[{\bm{q}}-{\bm{q}}^{\prime}],0}\delta_{\{{\bm{q}}-{\bm{q}}^{\prime}\},0}=\delta_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}.\end{split} $$

The expectation value of the two-particle operator $c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}$ can then be related to the structure factor in the following way:

$$ \begin{split}\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}\rangle=&\sum_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{p}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{\bm{p}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\langle\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}}\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{p}}\rangle=\sum_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{p}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{-{\bm{q}}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\langle\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}}\tilde{\rho}_{-{\bm{q}}}\rangle\delta_{{\bm{p}},-{\bm{q}}}\\
=&\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{-{\bm{q}}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}S_{\bm{q}}\\
=&\frac{1}{N_{G}^{2}}\sum_{\bm{q}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\delta_{[-{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\lambda_{{\bm{q}}}^{*}({\bm{k}}_{1})\lambda_{-{\bm{q}}}^{*}({\bm{k}}_{3})S_{\bm{q}}\\
=&\frac{1}{N_{G}^{2}}\sum_{\bm{q}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\delta_{[-{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\tilde{\lambda}_{{\bm{q}}}^{*}({\bm{k}}_{1})\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{-{\bm{q}}}({\bm{k}}_{3})S_{\bm{q}}.\end{split} $$

Let us now construct matrices that have indices ${\bm{q}}$ and ${\bm{k}}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}$ :

$$ [M_{12}]_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{q}}}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{G}}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{1}-{\bm{k}}_{2}],0}\tilde{\lambda}_{{\bm{q}}}^{*}({\bm{k}}_{1})\quad\text{and}\quad[M_{34}]_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{k}}_{3}{\bm{k}}_{4}}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{G}}\delta_{[-{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\tilde{\lambda}_{-{\bm{q}}}^{*}({\bm{k}}_{3}) $$

since there are $N_{G}^{2}$ numbers of ${\bm{q}}$ points and $N_{G}$ numbers of ${\bm{k}}$ points so that the matrices constructed are square. Using the same reasoning in Eqs. (S37),(S38), we find $M_{12}=M_{34}^{\dagger}$ and

$$ \begin{split}\left[M_{12}^{\dagger}M_{12}\right]_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{N_{G}}\delta_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{q}}^{\prime}},\qquad\left[M_{12}M_{12}^{\dagger}\right]_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}{\bm{k}}_{4}}=\frac{1}{N_{G}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}{\bm{k}}_{4}},\end{split} $$

where $\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}{\bm{k}}_{4}}\equiv\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{4}}$ . This follows from the fact that $\left[\delta_{[-{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\tilde{\lambda}_{-{\bm{q}}}^{*}({\bm{k}}_{3})\right]^{*}=\delta_{[-{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\tilde{\lambda}_{-{\bm{q}}}({\bm{k}}_{3})=\delta_{[-{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{k}}_{4}],0}\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{{\bm{q}}}({\bm{k}}_{3}-{\bm{q}})=\delta_{[{\bm{q}}+{\bm{k}}_{4}-{\bm{k}}_{3}],0}\tilde{\lambda}^{*}_{{\bm{q}}}({\bm{k}}_{4})$ , thus $\left[[M_{34}]_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{k}}_{3}{\bm{k}}_{4}}\right]^{*}=[M_{12}]_{{\bm{k}}_{4}{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{q}}}\Rightarrow M_{34}^{\dagger}=M_{12}$ . Be noted that the ${\bm{k}}$ labels are also flipped. Thus, $M_{12}$ $(M_{34})$ is actually a unitary matrix up to a constant scaling. In this sense, the two-particle expectation value is given by

$$ \langle c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}\rangle=\left[\sqrt{N_{\bm{G}}}M_{12}{\rm diag}[S_{\bm{q}}/N_{\bm{G}}]\sqrt{N_{\bm{G}}}M_{12}^{\dagger}\right]_{{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}{\bm{k}}_{4}}, $$

which is a unitary rotation of matrix ${\rm diag}[S_{\bm{q}}/N_{\bm{G}}]$ . Thus, $S_{\bm{q}}\geq 0$ for all ${\bm{q}}$ implies that the two-particle expectation value in the form of a matrix with indices ${\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}$ and ${\bm{k}}_{4}{\bm{k}}_{3}$ is necessarily positive semi-definite (PSD). This can be summarized as

$$ \langle c^{\dagger}cc^{\dagger}c\rangle\in\mathcal{H}^{N_{\bm{q}}}_{+}\Leftrightarrow S_{\bm{q}}\geq 0\quad\forall{\bm{q}}, $$

where $\mathcal{H}^{N_{q}}_{+}$ is the set of PSD hermitian matrices with dimension $N_{\bm{q}}\times N_{\bm{q}}$ .

However, for other types of four-fermion operators like $\langle ccc^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}\rangle$ and $\langle c^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}cc\rangle$ , this is in general not true. For example, let us consider the four-fermion operator $\langle c^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}cc\rangle$ . Notice that because of the fermionic anti-commutation relation, we should restrict the indices. We can define

$$ \mathcal{D}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}\equiv\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}\rangle, $$

where ${\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}$ just denotes a way of pairing ${\bm{k}}_{1}$ and ${\bm{k}}_{2}$ to avoid its reverse and bears no meaning of the magnitude comparison. By definition, the matrix $\mathcal{D}$ has a dimension $\frac{N_{\bm{k}}(N_{\bm{k}}-1)}{2}\times\frac{N_{\bm{k}}(N_{\bm{k}}-1)}{2}$ (note: $N_{\bm{q}}=N_{\bm{k}}^{2}=N_{\bm{G}}^{2}=N_{\Phi}^{2}$ ). Then, for a two-hole operator $\mathcal{O}_{1}=\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}A_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}$ , we have

$$ \langle\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\dagger}\mathcal{O}_{1}\rangle=\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}A^{*}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}}\mathcal{D}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}A_{{\bm{k}}_{3}{\bm{k}}_{4}}\geq 0\quad\forall A\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\bm{k}}(N_{\bm{k}}-1)/2}, $$

which means $\mathcal{D}\in\mathcal{H}^{N_{\bm{k}}(N_{\bm{k}}-1)/2}_{+}$ . Using the expressions derived above, we can rewrite the matrix $\mathcal{D}$ as

$$ \mathcal{D}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}=-\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}\rangle=\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}\rangle-\nu\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}=\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\Lambda^{-{\bm{q}}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}S_{\bm{q}}-\nu\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}. $$

In this case, $S_{\bm{q}}\geq 0$ implies nothing about the semi-definiteness of the matrix $\mathcal{D}$ which therefore acts non-trivially on the Bootstrapping process.

The other four-fermion operator $\langle ccc^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}\rangle$ is actually related to the above discussed one by the particle-hole symmetry and gives weaker constraints when $\nu<1/2$ and exactly the same constraints when $\nu=1/2$ . Let us define

$$ \mathcal{Q}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}\equiv\langle c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}\rangle, $$

which can be evaluated as

$$ \mathcal{Q}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}\rangle+(1-2\nu)\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{4}}-(1-\nu)\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}. $$

One can see imediately that $\mathcal{Q}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}(\nu=1/2)=\mathcal{D}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}(\nu=1/2)$ . To see this only gives weaker constraints for $\nu<1/2$ , we note that by the way we vectorized the coefficients $A_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}$ (or anti-symmetrization), $\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}$ is always zero since ${\bm{k}}_{2}={\bm{k}}_{3}$ and ${\bm{k}}_{1}={\bm{k}}_{4}$ are incompatible with the conditions ${\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}$ and ${\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}$ . Moreover, $\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{4}}$ is the identity matrix in our notation. So. all together, we have simply:

$$ \mathcal{Q}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}=\mathcal{D}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}+(1-2\nu)\mathcal{I}. $$

This means that, for $\nu<1/2$ , a positive semi-definite $\mathcal{D}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}$ always leads to a positive definite $\mathcal{Q}^{{\bm{k}}_{1}<{\bm{k}}_{2}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}<{\bm{k}}_{4}}$ .

#### A.3.2 GMP algebra in terms of inverse form factor matrix

The GMP algebra is also encoded in the inverse form factor matrix but in a much more complicated way. To see this, we first observe that

$$ c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}-c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}=c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{4}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}-c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}, $$

which then can be rewritten in terms of inverse form factor matrices:

$$ \sum_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{p}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{\bm{p}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\left[\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}},\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{p}}\right]=\sum_{{\bm{q}},{\bm{p}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{\bm{p}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\tilde{\rho}_{{\bm{q}}+{\bm{p}}}2i\sin\frac{{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{p}}}{2}=\sum_{\bm{q}}\left(\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}-\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\right)\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}}, $$

which can be rewritten as

$$ \sum_{\bm{q}}\left(\sum_{\bm{p}}\Lambda^{{\bm{q}}-{\bm{p}}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{\bm{p}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}2i\sin\frac{{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{p}}}{2}\right)\tilde{\rho}_{{\bm{q}}}=\sum_{\bm{q}}\left(\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}-\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\right)\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}},\quad\forall{\bm{k}}_{1,2,3,4}\in\text{BZ}. $$

Multiplying both sides by $\tilde{\rho}_{-{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}$ and taking the expectation value, we have

$$ \left(\sum_{\bm{p}}\Lambda^{{\bm{q}}-{\bm{p}}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{\bm{p}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}2i\sin\frac{{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{p}}}{2}\right)S_{{\bm{q}}}=\left(\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}-\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\right)S_{\bm{q}},\quad\forall{\bm{k}}_{1,2,3,4}\in\text{BZ}. $$

Notice that we have in general $S_{\bm{q}}>0$ , the GMP algebra becomes simply:

$$ \sum_{\bm{p}}\Lambda^{{\bm{q}}-{\bm{p}}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{\bm{p}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{4}}2i\sin\frac{{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{p}}}{2}=\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}-\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{4}},\quad\forall{\bm{k}}_{1,2,3,4}\in\text{BZ}. $$

One should be aware that this is not a constraint but a property of the inverse form factor matrix for the 0 ${}^{\text{th}}$ LL, since no $S_{\bm{q}}$ dependence is in it. This also means by using the inverse form factor matrix, the GMP algebra for the $S_{\bm{q}}$ (or 2RDM) is built in, and does not need to be implemented as a separate constraint.

Another way of seeing this is the following. Consider an arbitrary bilinear operator

$$ \hat{A}=\sum_{\alpha\beta}A_{\alpha\beta}c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}c_{\beta} $$

where $A$ denotes some operator, $\hat{A}$ is its second quantized representation and $A_{\alpha\beta}$ are its matrix elements in some basis. It is straightforward to show that $[\hat{A},\hat{B}]=\widehat{[A,B]}$ and that $\hat{A}=\hat{B}$ if and only if $A=B$ (which also means $A_{\alpha\beta}=B_{\alpha\beta}$ for all $\alpha$ and $\beta$ ). Furthermore, the form factors are the matrix representation of the density operator $\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{q}}=\hat{\Lambda}_{\bm{q}}$ . Thus, the GMP algebra implies

$$ \widehat{[\Lambda_{\bm{q}},\Lambda_{\bm{p}}]}=2i\sin\frac{{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{p}}}{2}\hat{\Lambda}_{{\bm{p}}+{\bm{q}}}\quad\leftrightarrow\quad[\Lambda_{\bm{q}},\Lambda_{\bm{p}}]=2i\sin\frac{{\bm{q}}\wedge{\bm{p}}}{2}\Lambda_{{\bm{p}}+{\bm{q}}} $$

where the last relation holds as an identity for the matrix elements. Thus, the GMP algebra is encoded in the form factor matrix. Then, one can use the relation between the form factor matrix and its inverse to get the expression (S54).

#### A.3.3 (2,3)-T1/T2 constraint

In this section, we want to impose the so-called (2,3)-T1 constraint which is deduced from convexly combining two three-particle positivity constraints to get a reduced constraint for two-particle expectation values. Consider the following two operators: $\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}=\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}A_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}=\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}A^{*}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}$ , we have the following positivity constraints:

$$ \langle\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}^{\dagger}\rangle\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\langle\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}^{\dagger}\rangle\geq 0, $$

as well as any convex combinations of the above two inequalities. It is not hard to see that

$$ \begin{split}\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}^{\dagger}&=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}\\
{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}\end{subarray}}A_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}}A^{*}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}}\\
&=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}\\
{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}\end{subarray}}A_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}}A^{*}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}}\left[-c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}+c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},[{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}]}\right.\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad-\left.c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2},[{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}]}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}}+\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3},[{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}]}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}}\right],\end{split} $$

where $\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{i},[{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}]}$ is defined as the sum of the cyclic permutations of the indices enclosed in the square bracket:

$$ \delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{i},[{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}]}\equiv\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{i},{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}+\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{i},{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}+\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{i},{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}. $$

Thus, the convex combination $\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}^{\dagger}+\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}^{\dagger}$ cancels exactly the three-particle terms. Then, the following constraint containing only at most two-particle terms

$$ \langle\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}^{\dagger}\rangle+\langle\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}^{\dagger}\rangle\geq 0,\quad\forall A_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}} $$

is the so-called (2,3)-T1 constraint.

By using the inverse form factor matrix, we can rewrite the (2,3)-T1 constraint in terms of the two-particle structure factor:

$$ \begin{split}&\langle\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}\mathcal{O}_{T1,1}^{\dagger}\rangle+\langle\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}\mathcal{O}_{T1,2}^{\dagger}\rangle\\
=&\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}\\
{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}\end{subarray}}A_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}}A^{*}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2}{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3}}\left[\left(-\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{-{\bm{q}}}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}S_{\bm{q}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{1}}+\nu\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{1}}+\left(\text{cyclic permutation of }{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}\right)\right)\right.\\
&-\left.\left(-\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{-{\bm{q}}}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}S_{\bm{q}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{1}}+\nu\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{1}}+\left(\text{cyclic permutation of }{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}\right)\right)\right.\\
&+\left.\left(-\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\Lambda^{\bm{q}}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\Lambda^{-{\bm{q}}}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}S_{\bm{q}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{1}}+(2\nu-1)\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{1}}+(1-\nu)\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2}}\delta_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}_{3},{\bm{k}}_{1}}+\left(\text{cyclic permutation of }{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}\right)\right)\right]\\
\geq&0,\quad\forall A_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}}\in\mathbb{C}.\end{split} $$

Like what has been discussed in the (2,2) positivity case, we can also antisymmetrize the indices to reduce the dimensionality of the matrix.

Similar to the (2,3)-T1 constraint discussed above, there is another simple (2,3)-positivity constraint bared the name (2,3)-T2 constraint as an extension to the T1, which involves the following two operators:

$$ \begin{split}\mathcal{O}_{T2,1}=&\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}A_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}+\sum_{\bm{k}}B_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}}\\
\mathcal{O}_{T2,2}=&\sum_{{\bm{k}}_{1},{\bm{k}}_{2},{\bm{k}}_{3}}A^{*}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}{\bm{k}}_{2}{\bm{k}}_{3}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{1}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}_{2}}c_{{\bm{k}}_{3}}+\sum_{\bm{k}}D^{*}_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}},\end{split} $$

which are really the generalized T2 operators. Following the same reasoning discussed above, we have $\mathcal{O}_{T2,1}\mathcal{O}_{T2,1}^{\dagger}+\mathcal{O}_{T2,2}\mathcal{O}_{T2,2}^{\dagger}$ cancels exactly the three-particle terms. Writing the (2,3)-T2 constraint using the structure factor and the inverse form factors is similar to what we did for the T1 case but more complicated, which will be omitted here. This procedure can then be extended to any (2,p)-positivity constraints.
